sections.h2: Does Missouri charge an estate tax?
sections.html:
Missouri imposes no estate tax for any death since the start of 2005, and no state return has to be filed for those deaths. The revenue department explains that the state tax was tied to a federal credit, and the IRS stopped allowing that credit for deaths after 2004.

The mechanism is in RSMo 145.011. It taxes the transfer of an estate with Missouri tax situs at the maximum state death tax credit under Internal Revenue Code Section 2011. Federal law stepped that credit down to 75 percent for 2002 deaths, 50 percent for 2003, 25 percent for 2004 and nothing afterward, which leaves the Missouri figure at zero. If the IRS ever brings the credit back, a Missouri return would be due again under sections 145.011 to 145.955.

sections.h2: Is there a federal estate tax that could reach a Missouri house?
sections.html:
Federal estate tax reaches only estates above the basic exclusion amount, which the IRS sets at $15,000,000 for 2026 deaths under the law signed on July 4, 2025. Most family homes in Missouri fall far below that line. A married couple can also carry over an unused exclusion to the surviving spouse by electing portability on a timely filed return.

Federal basic exclusion amount by year of death, from the IRS estate and gift tax page
Year of deathBasic exclusion amount
2022$12,060,000
2023$12,920,000
2024$13,610,000
2025$13,990,000
2026$15,000,000

An estate over the threshold files Form 706. When the executor files one, beneficiaries generally get a Schedule A on Form 8971 reporting the estate tax value of what they received, and certain beneficiaries must use that figure as initial basis.

sections.h2: How can heirs get an inherited Missouri house sold?
sections.html:
Which path fits depends on how big the estate is and whether a personal representative has been appointed. Two paths in the Missouri statutes cover most house sales by heirs.

Two Missouri routes to selling a decedent's real estate, based on the revisor's statutes
RouteWhat triggers itStatute
Small estate affidavitNet estate of $40,000 or less after liens and debts, thirty days since the death, and no pending or granted application for lettersRSMo 473.097
Petition to sellAn executor or administrator asks the probate court for authority to sell real property of the estateRSMo 473.493

On the small estate route, distributees show title by recording a copy of the affidavit and the clerk's certificate in every county that holds part of the land. The person signing the affidavit posts a bond unless the court waives it and pays the filing fee. If the listed property tops $15,000, the clerk runs a creditor notice two weeks in a row.

sections.h2: What does a court-ordered sale look like?
sections.html:
When letters have issued, RSMo 473.493 lets the executor or administrator file a petition stating why the sale is needed and describing the property. The court schedules a hearing and sends notice, by regular mail or publication, to heirs and devisees named in the file and to others the court names.

  • If the court orders publication, the notice runs weekly for four straight weeks.
  • The hearing then falls no earlier than the thirtieth day and no later than the forty-second day after the first insertion.
  • With satisfactory proof at the hearing, the court may approve a sale of the whole property or a piece of it.
  • When a mortgage secures a claim that is due, the court may order a sale subject to the mortgage with the lender's consent, and that consent releases the estate from any later deficiency.

Your probate attorney will tell you whether a petition is needed or whether the will already gives the personal representative power to sell.

sections.h2: Do heirs need an IRS closing letter or basis statement before a sale?
sections.html:
Only estates that must file Form 706 deal with these items. For those estates, Section 6035 requires the executor to send statements to the IRS and to beneficiaries who receive certain property, and Section 1014(f) requires the beneficiary's basis to stay consistent with the value finally determined for federal estate tax. The IRS issued final regulations on this consistent basis reporting on September 16, 2024.

An estate that is not required to file a return should not send Form 8971, because the IRS warns that doing so may cause unnecessary correspondence.

An executor who wants proof that the federal case is closed can request the Estate Tax Closing Letter, Letter 627. The IRS raised the user fee for that letter from $56 to $76 on October 26, 2026, so the higher amount now applies. Heirs waiting on a sale of the family house should ask the executor whether a return was filed and, if so, request their Schedule A before the closing date so the buyer's price and your basis figure can be matched to the paperwork.

sections.h2: What tax do heirs pay after selling an inherited Missouri house?
sections.html:
The federal gain is the sale price less basis, and basis for inherited property is generally the house's worth when the owner died, under IRS Publication 551. A house worth $200,000 at death and sold for $205,000 shows $5,000 of gain, regardless of what the original owner paid decades earlier. The IRS directs readers who inherited property to Publication 551 and to Topic 409 for holding period details.

On the state side, Missouri lets an individual subtract all federally reported capital gains when computing the state return. That subtraction is available to individuals and not to trusts, so who holds title when the sale closes matters. If the sale happens inside the estate, ask the preparer how the estate's income is reported.

Missouri imposes a fiduciary income tax on income earned by an estate or trust. A resident estate that must file federal Form 1041 files a Missouri fiduciary return, and a nonresident estate must file when it has $600 or more of Missouri-source gross income.

sections.h2: What paperwork should heirs gather before listing?
sections.html:
• A certified death certificate, since the date of death anchors the basis figure.
  • Letters testamentary or of administration, or the small estate affidavit with the clerk's certificate.
  • An appraisal or other documented fair market value as of the date of death.
  • The current deed, which carries the legal description the recorder will need.
  • Any Schedule A from Form 8971, if the estate filed a federal return.
  • Payoff figures for any mortgage, unpaid tax or lien.

A deed goes on file with the recorder of the county that holds the land under RSMo 442.380. RSMo 442.400 adds that an unrecorded instrument is valid only between the parties and anyone with actual notice, so the buyer's deed should be filed promptly. A probate attorney near the decedent's home court can confirm the filing order for your estate.

faqs.q: Is there a Missouri estate tax for deaths in 2026?
faqs.a: No. The revenue department reports that no Missouri estate tax applies to any death since 2005, and no return is required. A return would be required again only if the IRS reinstated the federal state death tax credit.

faqs.q: How large must an estate be before federal estate tax applies?
faqs.a: For 2026 deaths the IRS basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000. An estate below that amount owes no federal estate tax, although a surviving spouse may still file to elect portability of an unused amount.

faqs.q: Can heirs sell a Missouri house without opening probate?
faqs.a: Sometimes. When the net estate is $40,000 or under, thirty days have gone by and no one has sought letters, distributees can use the small estate affidavit in RSMo 473.097 and file it with the recorder.

faqs.q: What is the tax basis of a house I inherited?
faqs.a: Generally what it was worth at the owner's death, or on the alternate valuation date if the estate chose one. Beneficiaries of an estate that filed Form 706 usually receive a Schedule A with the value.

faqs.q: Does Missouri tax the gain when an heir sells an inherited house?
faqs.a: Eligible individuals may subtract all federally reported capital gains on the state return, using Form MO-A with Form MO-1040. Trusts cannot claim that subtraction.
